sources.title: An Experiment in Paper Virtual Money Museum Exhibit
sources.locator: An Experiment in Paper exhibit text, web lines 30–34, especially the Sichuan private notes and government nationalization at lines 32–33. Public HTML read.
sources.originalChronology: The exhibit dates government nationalization of paper currency to 1023, after private jiaozi and merchant standardization in Sichuan. Its separate Huizi discussion concerns 1160 and is not included.
sources.scopedClaim: Song authorities took over a paper-note system developed by merchants in Sichuan. This is an administrative transition, not a claim that paper or printing was invented then.

sources.title: 紙幣早於何時面世？
sources.institution: Chinese Culture Institute; Dr Lin Feng (林楓博士), 7 February 2020
sources.locator: Authored educational article, web lines 123–128 for private notes and the Yizhou Jiaozi Office; lines 137–143 identify the author and publication date. Public Chinese HTML read.
sources.originalChronology: The opening gives Tiansheng 2 (1024) for jiaozi, while the administrative passage dates the Yizhou Jiaozi Office to Tiansheng 1 (1023). The text also describes earlier private notes. These statements are retained without resolving their different chronological framing.
sources.scopedClaim: The Song government established an office at Yizhou to manage official jiaozi issuance, principally for Sichuan. The candidate does not adopt the article's absolute earliest-paper-money claim.
sources.reuseTerms: Reference only; no source prose or images redistributed

sources.title: 东西问丨刘方健、罗天云：人类最早的纸币交子为何诞生在成都？
sources.institution: China News Service; Wang Peng interviews Liu Fangjian and Luo Tianyun, 13 December 2024
sources.locator: Public interview transcript, web lines 43–53: Luo Tianyun's answer on the dating of official jiaozi; line 53 distinguishes approval on 12 January 1024 from issuance on 1 April 1024. Lines 92–98 identify the interviewees. These dates belong to Luo's answer, not Liu's.
sources.originalChronology: Luo Tianyun dates court approval of the Yizhou Jiaozi Office to 12 January 1024 and formal issuance to 1 April 1024. This is a published researcher's interview account; the underlying decree and the interviewees' book were not inspected. No calendar conversion is made.
sources.scopedClaim: A named researcher supplies an alternative 1024 chronology for official administration and issuance. Luo is identified as a jiaozi researcher and coauthor, not as the university professor named in the interview. The candidate preserves this attribution and does not treat the interview as a directly inspected Song decree.

date.displayEn: AD 1023–1024; accounts differ on the administrative date
date.noteEn: The ANA dates government takeover to 1023, and Lin Feng dates the Yizhou office to 1023. In a later published interview, Luo Tianyun instead gives 12 January 1024 for court approval and 1 April 1024 for official issuance. These source dates are preserved without an independent calendar conversion or a claim that every step occurred in both years.

events.titleEn: Song authorities take over jiaozi issuance in Sichuan
events.summaryEn: Song authorities bring a paper-note system developed by Sichuan merchants under government administration. The Yizhou Jiaozi Office manages official issuance, marking a change in who controls the notes. The sources differ over the date of the administrative transition.
events.selectionNote: A major regional change in monetary administration, separate from later Ming paper-money issuance and Wang Anshi's reforms. Accounts place takeover or office establishment in 1023, while Luo's interview gives approval on 12 January 1024 and issuance on 1 April 1024; the underlying decree was not read. No invention of paper, worldwide priority, modern central bank, or immediate extension across all Song territory is claimed.
